cards.prompt: 1st Gen - Antipsychotics Typical / Conventional DISADVANTAGE → More EPS! ←
cards.promptHtml:
1st Gen - Antipsychotics

Typical / Conventional

DISADVANTAGE

→ More EPS! ←
cards.answerHtml:
ACTION

  • block dopamine D2

NAMES

High potency:

haloperidol (Haldol) → [Tourette tics] → works immediately] → raised prolactin

fluphenazine (Prolixin),

thiothixene (Navane),

pimozide (Orap). → Tourette tics

Low potency:

chlorpromazine (Thorazine), → nausea/intractable hiccups

thioridazine (Mellaril)

TIMING

  • ~1-2 weeks for changes
  • 6-12 week trials during stabilization

USES

  • Schizophrenia,
  • acute psychosis,
  • mania,
  • agitation;

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • EPS (dystonia, pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia)
  • tardive dyskinesia

[mainly with high potency]

  • anticholinergic effects,
  • sedation,
  • orthostatic hypotension,
  • photosensitivity and skin discoloration (low potency),
  • lowered seizure threshold,
  • raised prolactin (galactorrhea, amenorrhea, sexual dysfunction - esp w/ haloperidol)
  • QTc prolongation
  • [Might cause emotional numbness]

MONITORING / LABS

  • AIMS at least every 3–6 months;
  • temperature (NMS);
  • orthostatic BP;
  • ECG if cardiac risk;
  • watch for EPS from the first dose

TEACHING

  • Antipsychotics cause sedation
  • → fall risk!
  • Rise slowly;
  • sunscreen and protective clothing;
  • report stiffness, restlessness, tongue or face movements;
  • do not stop abruptly;
  • avoid alcohol

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Fever + rigidity + confusion (NMS);
  • laryngeal spasm or oculogyric crisis (acute dystonia);
  • new tongue/lip movements (TD)

cards.prompt: 2nd Gen - Antipsychotics Atypical DISADVANTAGE = More metabolic effects
cards.answerHtml:
ACTION:

  • Block
  • Serotonin
  • Glutamate
  • Dopamine

NAMES

  • Risperidone (Risperdal),
  • olanzapine (Zyprexa),
  • quetiapine (Seroquel), → Elderly use it to help them sleep
  • ziprasidone (Geodon), → DRESS rash [fever, swollen lymphs, rash] → with 350 cal of food
  • aripiprazole (Abilify),
  • paliperidone (Invega),
  • lurasidone (Latuda), → Bipolar w/ psychosis [IM] → with 350 cal of food
  • asenapine (Saphris),
  • brexpiprazole (Rexulti),
  • cariprazine (Vraylar) → schizoaffective disorder, helps w/ psychosis, Less likely to cause weight gain

USES

  • Schizophrenia,
  • bipolar mania and maintenance,
  • adjunct in depression,
  • autism irritability

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Metabolic syndrome:
  • weight gain (worst with clozapine and olanzapine, up to 20 lb in 1 year),
  • May give metformin to help
  • type 2 diabetes (FDA: all atypicals raise risk),
  • dyslipidemia;
  • less EPS and TD than typicals;
  • prolactin rise
  • orthostasis;
  • QTc;
  • [Might cause emotional numbness]

MONITORING / LABS

  • Weight / BMI
  • monthly × 3 months then quarterly;
  • [Overweight = BMI > 25]
  • [BAD = cholesterol > 200]
  • waist circumference;
  • BP,
  • fasting glucose,
  • [prediabetes = over 100
  • [Diabetic = > 126]
  • fasting lipids at baseline, within 3 months, then yearly
  • [Normal HgbA1C
  • < 5.6 / 5.7
  • [5.7 - 6.5 = Prediabetic
  • 6.5 > is Diabetic]

TEACHING

  • Diet and exercise from day one;
  • Report
  • thirst,
  • frequent urination,
  • weight gain;
  • smoking changes blood levels of some agents
  • Antipsychotics cause sedation
  • → fall risk!
  • Rise slowly

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Polyuria/polydipsia/fatigue (hyperglycemia);
  • NMS signs;
  • boxed warning: increased death in elderly with dementia-related psychosis

NAME

  • Clozapine

USES

  • reserved for treatment-resistant illness
  • Schizophrenia that failed other antipsychotics;
  • reduces recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Agranulocytosis/severe neutropenia (cumulative 1-year incidence about 1.3%, most often weeks 4–10; highest risk first 18 weeks);
  • seizures;
  • myocarditis;
  • orthostatic hypotension;
  • hypersalivation;
  • severe weight gain;
  • constipation;
  • tachycardia;
  • fever

MONITORING / LABS

  • Blood counts before starting, weekly for 6 months, every 2 weeks for months 6–12, then monthly
  • the book states weekly × 6 months then every 2 weeks, and continue for 4 weeks after stopping
  • Start only if WBC >3,500/mm³; monitor 3×/week if WBC 3,500–5,000;
  • stop if WBC <3,500 or granulocytes <1,500;
  • agranulocytosis = granulocytes <500/mm³ (often <200)
  • [Normal ANC 1,500-8,000]

TEACHING

  • Informed consent about blood draws;
  • report sore throat, fever, flu-like symptoms, lethargy immediately;
  • change positions slowly;
  • avoid alcohol;
  • do not stop abruptly;
  • seizures can occur, so no driving early in titration

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Any fever or sore throat: hold dose until a count is obtained
  • chest pain/dyspnea (myocarditis);
  • seizure;
  • severe constipation/abdominal distension (ileus)

NAMES

  • Haloperidol decanoate (q3–4 wk),
  • fluphenazine decanoate (q2–3 wk),
  • risperidone (Risperdal Consta q2 wk; Perseris monthly SC) → prolactin rise
  • paliperidone (Invega Sustenna monthly),
  • aripiprazole (Abilify Maintena; Aristada),
  • olanzapine (Relprevv q2–4 wk) → can cause post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome

USES

  • Maintenance for patients with poor adherence;
  • steady blood levels between injections

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Same as the oral drug;
  • injection-site pain/inflammation;
  • depot use is a risk factor for NMS
  • (general knowledge: 3-hour observation required)

MONITORING / LABS

  • Same as oral;
  • inspect injection site

TEACHING

  • Keep every injection appointment;
  • side effects may last weeks after a dose

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Oil-based (haloperidol, fluphenazine decanoate):
  • at least 21-gauge needle, dry needle, deep IM Z-track, do not massage, rotate sites

TIMING

  • ~2 weeks to take effect (full effect in about ~6 weeks)
  • Continue 6-12 months after remission

NAMES

  • Fluoxetine (Prozac),
  • sertraline (Zoloft), → PTSD
  • paroxetine (Paxil), → PTSD → insomnia or sedation
  • citalopram (Celexa),
  • escitalopram (Lexapro),
  • fluvoxamine (Luvox)

USES

  • Depression,
  • anxiety disorders,
  • OCD,
  • eating disorders
  • panic,
  • Social phobia,

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Nausea,
  • Headache,
  • anxiety/jitteriness early, diarrhea,
  • sexual dysfunction (anorgasmia, ejaculation problems),
  • sweating;
  • hyponatremia in older adults (general knowledge);
  • serotonin syndrome in combination

MONITORING / LABS

  • Suicidal thinking, especially early and with dose changes (boxed warning for children, adolescents, young adults);
  • mood;
  • sodium in older adults

TEACHING

  • Takes 1–4+ weeks for effect (some improvement in about 7 days, full relief may take several weeks);
  • take in the morning unless sedating;
  • never stop abruptly—taper (discontinuation syndrome);
  • no → St. John's wort, triptans, or other serotonergic drugs without approval
  • at least 14 days between an MAOI and an SSRI
  • (5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI)

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Agitation + fever + tremor/clonus + diaphoresis + hyperreflexia + diarrhea (serotonin syndrome);
  • new suicidal ideation or sudden "energy" in a depressed patient (general knowledge);

NAMES

  • Venlafaxine (Effexor), → discontinuation is notoriously unpleasant
  • desvenlafaxine (Pristiq),
  • duloxetine (Cymbalta), → neuropathic pain
  • levomilnacipran (Fetzima)
  • nefazodone: boxed warning for liver failure

USES

  • Depression,
  • anxiety,

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • SSRI-like effects plus dose-related increase in blood pressure

MONITORING / LABS

  • Blood pressure, especially with hypertension history

TEACHING

  • Taper slowly

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Sustained hypertension;
  • serotonin syndrome;

NAMES

  • Amitriptyline (Elavil),
  • imipramine (Tofranil),
  • nortriptyline (Pamelor), → blood levels
  • desipramine (Norpramin),
  • doxepin (Sinequan),
  • clomipramine (Anafranil) → OCD

USES

  • Depression (now second-line),
  • chronic pain and insomnia at low dose

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Sedation,
  • orthostatic hypotension,
  • anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion),
  • cardiotoxicity (conduction delay, arrhythmia),
  • seizures,
  • weight gain

MONITORING / LABS

  • Baseline ECG, especially in older or cardiac patients (general knowledge);
  • orthostatic BP;
  • blood levels exist for some TCAs
  • (e.g., nortriptyline 50–150 ng/mL)

TEACHING

  • Give at bedtime if sedating
  • rise slowly;
  • fluids/fiber for constipation;
  • high lethality in overdose—dispense limited supplies to suicidal patients

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Contraindicated with 2nd-degree AV block
  • overdose = arrhythmias, seizures, coma; fever/sore throat (blood dyscrasia)

*Antidote = IV sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening (commonly >100 ms), dysrhythmias, or hypotension; plus airway, cardiac monitoring, charcoal only if the airway is protected, benzodiazepines for seizures; avoid physostigmine and flumazenil

  • Boyd lists induced emesis and gastric lavage*

NAMES

  • Phenelzine (Nardil),
  • tranylcypromine (Parnate),
  • isocarboxazid (Marplan),
  • selegiline transdermal (Emsam) → 6 mg/24 h patch is the only dose with no diet restriction

USES

  • Treatment-resistant or atypical depression

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • (falls in older adults), dizziness,
  • insomnia,
  • weight gain,
  • sexual dysfunction,
  • edema;
  • hypertensive crisis with tyramine or sympathomimetics

MONITORING / LABS

  • Lying and standing BP;
  • diet adherence

TEACHING

  • Tyramine-restricted diet
  • (see Lab/Emergency sections) during use and for at least 2 weeks after stopping (enzyme inhibition takes at least 2 weeks to resolve);
  • avoid OTC cold remedies,
  • diet pills,
  • decongestants;
  • tell every provider and dentist;
  • no meperidine

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Sudden severe occipital headache,
  • stiff neck,
  • palpitations,
  • chest pain,
  • sweating,
  • vomiting,
  • HTN = hypertensive crisis

*Antidote = phentolamine [for HTN crisis]

NAMES

  • Bupropion (Wellbutrin; Zyban for smoking), → ADHD, when sexual side effects are a problem
  • [do NOT take Wellbutrin & Zyban together]
  • mirtazapine (Remeron), → take at bedtime
  • trazodone (Desyrel),
  • vilazodone (Viibryd),
  • vortioxetine (Trintellix, formerly Brintellix),
  • esketamine nasal spray (Spravato)

USES

  • Depression

Bupropion:

  • SE
  • activation,
  • insomnia,
  • appetite loss,
  • seizures (contraindicated in seizure disorders and eating disorders) = HOLD!
  • rarely psychosis;
  • low sexual dysfunction.

Mirtazapine:

  • SE
  • Sedation,
  • appetite
  • weight gain.

Trazodone:

  • SE
  • sedation,
  • orthostasis,
  • Priapism = HOLD!

Esketamine:

  • SE:
  • dissociation,
  • sedation,
  • BP rise,
  • abuse potential
  • Nursing
  • given only under supervision,
  • BP before and after,
  • observe after dose;
  • no food 2 h before,
  • no liquids 30 min before
  • No driving

TIMING

  • Takes
  • Days → weeks
  • onset 5–7 days to 2 weeks;

NAMES

  • Lithium (Eskalith, Lithobid)
  • Lithium carbonate;
  • lithium citrate liquid

USES

  • Gold standard for acute mania and bipolar maintenance;
  • reduces suicide risk

ADVERSE EFFECTS

Common:

  • thirst,
  • metallic taste,
  • polyuria,
  • fine hand tremor,
  • nausea,
  • mild diarrhea,
  • weight gain (~20%),
  • acne,
  • psoriasis flare;

Long-term:

  • hypothyroidism (after 6–18 months),
  • kidney damage, hypercalcemia;
  • teratogen

MONITORING / LABS

  • Serum level 12 hours after last dose (hold the morning dose until drawn);
  • levels 2x weekly in acute phase, every 2–3 months in maintenance;
  • creatinine, TSH/thyroid, CBC every 6 months

TEACHING

  • Keep sodium and fluid intake steady; drink adequate fluids (2–3 L/day)
  • dehydration from heat, exercise, fever, vomiting, or diarrhea raises levels;
  • avoid
  • NSAIDs,
  • thiazide diuretics,
  • ACE inhibitors unless prescriber approves;
  • avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding;
  • abrupt stop causes relapse in almost half

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Toxicity = hold dose, draw level, call prescriber:
  • Coarse tremor,
  • vomiting,
  • severe diarrhea,
  • drowsiness,
  • ataxia,
  • slurred speech,
  • confusion

cards.prompt: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizers Mood Stabilizer + Antidepressant = Protect against manic switching
cards.promptHtml:
Anticonvulsant mood stabilizers

Mood Stabilizer + Antidepressant =

Protect against manic switching
cards.answerHtml:
NAMES

  • Divalproex/valproic acid (Depakote, Depakene), → Bipolar mania, mixed and rapid-cycling episodes
  • carbamazepine (Tegretol, Equetro), → lithium nonresponders
  • lamotrigine (Lamictal); → bipolar depression and maintenance

also used:

  • oxcarbazepine (Trileptal),
  • topiramate (Topamax),
  • gabapentin (Neurontin)

USES

  • Bipolar
  • Tx resistant depression

Valproate:

SE

  • GI upset,
  • tremor,
  • sedation,
  • weight gain,
  • hair loss,
  • thrombocytopenia;
  • boxed:
  • hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity,
  • Pancreatitis.

MONITOR

  • baseline LFTs and CBC with platelets;
  • level weekly until stable, then every 6 months;
  • amylase if abdominal pain.
  • Level =
  • 50 - 100

Carbamazepine:

SE

  • dizziness,
  • drowsiness,
  • nausea;
  • boxed: aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis; hyponatremia (SIADH);
  • severe rash;
  • many drug interactions (induces its own metabolism and lowers oral contraceptive levels).

MONITOR

  • LFTs and CBC with differential at baseline,
  • 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, then yearly;
  • levels monthly until stable;
  • Sodium
  • Level =
  • 8 - 12

REPORT

  • Use w/ non-hormonal birth control

HOLD

  • RASH
  • Fever / sore throat

Lamotrigine:

SE

  • boxed: life-threatening rash (Stevens–Johnson), usually weeks 2–8

TEACHING

  • Dose must be lowered if valproate is added

REPORT & HOLD

  • Rash

*Report FOR ALL*

  • fever,
  • sore throat,
  • bruising,
  • petechiae,
  • jaundice,
  • abdominal pain;

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain (liver);
  • severe abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting (pancreatitis);

TIMING

  • Oral = 30-60 min to take effect
  • IV = 15-30 min or quicker

ANXIOLYTIC

  • Lorazepam (Ativan), → for etoh withdrawal / older adults / liver disease
  • alprazolam (Xanax),
  • diazepam (Valium),
  • chlordiazepoxide (Librium),
  • clonazepam (Klonopin),
  • oxazepam (Serax), → for older adults / liver disease
  • clorazepate (Tranxene);

HYPNOTICS:

  • temazepam (Restoril),
  • triazolam (Halcion),
  • flurazepam (Dalmane)

USES

  • Short-term anxiety and panic,
  • alcohol withdrawal, agitation,
  • akathisia,
  • insomnia,
  • seizures

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Drowsiness,
  • impaired memory and coordination,
  • ataxia,
  • "hangover,"
  • falls and confusion in older adults (paradoxical agitation),
  • tolerance and dependence;
  • dangerous with alcohol and opioids;
  • birth defects risk

MONITORING / LABS

  • Sedation level,
  • respiratory status when combined with other CNS depressants,
  • fall risk,
  • signs of misuse

TEACHING

  • Avoid alcohol and driving;
  • do not stop abruptly—taper;
  • short-term use only;
  • DON’T drive!
  • May affect ability to swallow

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

Withdrawal / Abrupt stop after long use →

  • rebound anxiety,
  • tremor,
  • sweating,
  • rising BP,
  • seizures
  • respiratory depression when mixed with alcohol/opioids;

*antidote = flumazenil

NAME

  • Buspirone (BuSpar)

TIMING

  • Response after 2–4 weeks of regular dosing

ACTION

  • 5-HT1A action

USES

  • Generalized anxiety disorder;
  • anxiety with depression;
  • no effect on panic

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Dizziness,
  • drowsiness,
  • nausea,
  • headache,
  • excitement;
  • no sedation, no dependence, no abuse potential

TEACHING

  • Not PRN—must be taken regularly, usually TID;
  • does not prevent benzodiazepine withdrawal, so switching must be gradual;
  • avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Digoxin toxicity
  • (buspirone displaces digoxin)

NAMES

  • Hydroxyzine (Vistaril, Atarax)

USES

  • Anxiety,
  • itching,
  • nausea,
  • sleep

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Sedation,
  • dizziness,
  • anticholinergic effects,
  • possible QTc prolongation

MONITORING / LABS

  • Sedation;
  • avoid in older adults

TEACHING

  • Non-habit-forming alternative to benzodiazepines

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Confusion in older adults

NAMES

  • Zolpidem (Ambien),
  • eszopiclone (Lunesta),
  • zaleplon (Sonata);
  • ramelteon (Rozerem),
  • melatonin;
  • suvorexant (Belsomra);
  • doxylamine (Unisom)

USES

  • Insomnia

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Next-day drowsiness,
  • complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleepwalking) with "Z-drugs"
  • dizziness

MONITORING / LABS

  • Fall risk,
  • sleep pattern

TEACHING

  • Take immediately before bed with 7–8 hours available;
  • no alcohol;
  • short-term use

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Complex sleep behaviors

NAMES

  • Memantine (Namenda);
  • memantine + donepezil (Namzaric)

USES

  • Moderate to severe Alzheimer disease

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Dizziness,
  • headache,
  • confusion,
  • constipation

MONITORING / LABS

  • Cognition,
  • ADLs

TEACHING

  • Many drug interactions—check all new drugs

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Worsening confusion

NAMES

  • Donepezil (Aricept), → usually at bedtime
  • rivastigmine (Exelon, oral or patch),
  • galantamine (Razadyne)

USES

  • Alzheimer disease; delays decline, does not restore lost function, so start early

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Nausea,
  • vomiting,
  • diarrhea,
  • weight loss;
  • bradycardia and syncope

MONITORING / LABS

  • Weight,
  • GI tolerance,
  • pulse

TEACHING

  • Long-term NSAID use raises ulcer risk;

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • Syncope,
  • slow pulse,
  • GI bleeding

NAMES

  • Benztropine (Cogentin),
  • trihexyphenidyl (Artane),
  • biperiden;
  • diphenhydramine (Benadryl);
  • amantadine (Symmetrel)

USES

  • EPS
  • Acute dystonia (IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine),
  • pseudoparkinsonism;
  • less effective for akathisia

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Dry mouth,
  • blurred vision,
  • constipation,
  • urinary retention,
  • raised eye pressure,
  • confusion and delirium in older adults;
  • can be abused for euphoria

MONITORING / LABS

  • Bowel and bladder function,
  • mental status,
  • intraocular pressure in glaucoma

TEACHING

  • Sugar-free candy and sips of water,
  • fiber and fluids,
  • void regularly,
  • sunglasses
  • taper—abrupt stop can cause cholinergic rebound
  • (vomiting, sweating, nightmares)

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

anticholinergic crisis =

  • Hot,
  • dry,
  • flushed,
  • confused,
  • dilated pupils
  • urinary retention;
  • eye pain

NAMES

  • Propranolol (Inderal)

USES

  • Akathisia;
  • performance/situational anxiety; → can take 30-60 min before something, like public speaking
  • lithium tremor;
  • adjunct for aggression
  • PTSD

ADVERSE EFFECTS

  • Hypotension,
  • bradycardia,
  • fatigue;
  • masks hypoglycemia;
  • bronchospasm in ASTHMA! [contraindicated]

MONITORING / LABS

  • HR
  • BP

TEACHING

  • Do not stop abruptly [TAPER]
  • (rebound tachycardia)

RED FLAGS = HOLD & CALL MD

  • HR <50–60 or symptomatic hypotension
  • wheezing

cards.prompt: Treatment for: TD Dystonia Akathisia [late onset/challenging to treat]
cards.answerHtml:
Valbenazine &

Deutetrabenazine

[FDA-approved agents for tardive dyskinesia that reduce dopamine transport into storage vesicles]

Nursing

  • Stop the serotonergic drugs;
  • notify prescriber;
  • VS;
  • mild cases—
  • supportive care (propranolol, lorazepam);
  • Moderate–severe—
  • hospitalize, IV fluids, antipyretics, cooling blanket;
  • Severe = Antidote!
  • cyproheptadine (antiserotonergic)

HTN CRISIS:

S&S

  • Sudden severe occipital or temporal ("explosive") headache,
  • stiff/sore neck,
  • palpitations,
  • flushing,
  • chest pain,
  • nausea and vomiting,
  • sweating,
  • marked hypertension;
  • can cause stroke and death

Nursing

  • Hold MAOI;
  • check BP frequently;
  • notify prescriber immediately;
  • keep patient upright and quiet;
  • anticipate IV antihypertensive
  • (phentolamine is the classic answer) (general knowledge for phentolamine)

Anticholinergic toxicity (crisis)

S&S

  • "Hot as a hare, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, dry as a bone" (also "red as a beet"): fever; hot, dry, flushed skin;
  • dilated nonreactive pupils, blurred vision;
  • dry mouth, burning thirst;
  • tachycardia;
  • decreased bowel sounds;
  • urinary retention;
  • confusion,
  • agitation,
  • visual hallucinations with picking motions,
  • delirium,
  • seizures,
  • coma

Nursing

  • Stop the offending drug, notify prescriber;
  • antidote physostigmine 1–2 mg IV slowly over 5 minutes
  • (fast push → seizures, bradycardia, heart block; short acting, may repeat);
  • gastric lavage / charcoal for overdose;
  • cooling;
  • safety;
  • usually improves within 24–36 hours of stopping

Agranulocytosis

S&S

  • Sore throat,
  • fever,
  • mouth sores,
  • malaise,
  • flu-like symptoms;
  • counts may drop over just 2–3 days

Nursing

  • Hold the drug until a WBC/ANC is drawn;
  • notify prescriber;
  • infection precautions (reverse isolation may be needed);
  • counts usually recover in 2–4 weeks after stopping

Acute dystonia

S&S

  • Thick tongue
  • jaw tightness,
  • stiff neck → torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonos, laryngopharyngeal spasm with breathing difficulty

Nursing

  • Airway first;
  • give benztropine or diphenhydramine IM/IV as ordered;
  • stay with and reassure the patient (frightening but treatable)

Benzodiazepine withdrawal

S&S

  • Rebound anxiety and insomnia,
  • tremor,
  • sweating,
  • palpitations,
  • light sensitivity,
  • abdominal pain,
  • rising systolic BP;
  • can progress to seizures

Nursing

  • Never stop abruptly—taper gradually;
  • prescriber may switch to a long-acting benzodiazepine first;
  • seizure precautions

Water intoxication (psychogenic polydipsia)

S&S

  • Low serum sodium,
  • confusion,
  • headache,
  • vomiting,
  • seizures;
  • rapid weight gain

Nursing

  • Monitor weights and intake,
  • restrict fluids per order,
  • check sodium;
  • seizure precautions
